$comment: Who says which words in this chapter (docs/voice-narration-plan.md section 3). Drafted by `npm run voice:script`; a line with no entry is read by the narrator. A person checks each draft and sets `reviewed` to true; re-drafting only touches missing and stale entries.

lines.text: A prospector named Dunmore has planted his claim flag on the grandmother's doorstep.
"It hums!"
he says. So does every stone up here. She rings louder. He goes pink, but keeps his pick. Her house has a round window with curtains.

You climb onto the step beside the grandmother and plant your feet. Nobody can dig up a doorstep with people standing on it. Dunmore looks at your boots, then at the little round window with curtains in it, and goes pinker than ever.
"Sorry,"
he mumbles, and pulls up his flag. The grandmother gives him a cookie. He is so surprised that he says thank you twice.
Your dragonling stands on the step and says the rule every dragonling door knows:
"Take what the mountain drops. Never pry at what it holds."
Dunmore takes off his hat.
"Nobody told me,"
he says quietly, and writes it inside his hat.
Embermoths huddle on the cold side of a rock, away from the warm cracks they love. One refuses to leave a prospector's soup.
"I give up,"
he says, and eats around it.
"Moths leaving the warm is a warning,"
says your dragonling, in a grandmother voice. A grandmother three tents away hears it and rings her hand bell once, sharp, toward the next town.
Cinder wolves lie heaped in the road like coals with ears, too cold and hungry to care about the wagons.
"Off the road, you silly coals!"
shouts a centaur drover. Every drover is shouting. Nobody is moving.
Up the road, two prospectors stand on one humming boulder, each with a flag.
"Mine,"
says the burrowfolk.
"Mine,"
says the faun. They have tied their bootlaces to their flags. The crowd has brought snacks.
You hold up the Unassigned Stone and tell them about the grandmothers' old list of caves that belong to nobody.
"Nobody's,"
says one prospector, trying the word.
"Nobody's,"
says the other. They go and share a sandwich instead.

At the top of the road, a soup tent says FREE, NO QUESTIONS. A woman called Hessa Wren ladles soup for {party} and remembers every name. Helpers in painted bark masks stir the pots, humming one low note.
"My friends from the Deep Hollow,"
she says. Then, kindly:
"There's a seal on the mountain, like a lid on a pot. It's a cage on the cure. Will you help us open it?"
"You met Wend!"
Hessa's face lights up.
"Wend sends love to everybody, but Wend did say your names."
She adds an extra spoonful to each bowl. It is the same soup. Somehow it tastes like the whole road north.
Your kitsune nods at the bark mask in Hessa's apron pocket. She does not hide it.
"For singing. The mountain likes a choir."
She hums three notes, and the stones of the hillside hum back. She smiles like a gardener at a seedling.
You just eat the soup. It is excellent, with barley and something green. Hessa watches kindly and patiently. When you hand back the bowls, she says,
"Tomorrow, then,"
as if you had an appointment.
"No, thank you,"
you say. Hessa does not argue, does not stop smiling, and does not take the bowl back.
"The soup isn't the pitch,"
she says.
"The soup is just soup."
You believe her about the soup.
Hessa thinks about it properly.
"Who gets to be hungry,"
she says at last.
"Who gets to be cold. Why the sky is the wrong color, and nobody with a ledger can say why."
She refills your bowl.
"Little things. Everything."
Dragonling neighbors offer you warm stones to sleep on. Their bell-keeper, Grandmother Tull, rings the night bell. A spare bell sits beside it, never rung.
"That one is nothing to worry about,"
she says, and then says it again.
In the morning, Grandmother Tull teaches tiny dragonlings the bell calls on a bench. The spare bell is wrapped in a sock.
"Nothing to worry about,"
says Tull. Up the ridge, the citadel watch is listening.
Grandmother Tull takes a long breath.
"That one has never been rung. Everybody knows what it would mean, and nobody says it."
She pats the sock like a sleeping dog.
"Nothing to worry about."
That is four times now. She does not quite look at you.
On the ridge, Dunmore raises his pick at a glittering heap.
"It hums!"
The heap has eyes and claws. It is a glassback crab, rocking on its warm ground. Another watches from the next burrow. Dunmore should really check for curtains first.
"Dunmore! Three big steps back!"
He knows your voice now. He stops mid-swing and steps back, and the whole crowd steps back with him. The crab lowers its claws and goes back to tidying its pebbles.
Every window in Redspire Citadel faces up. Inside, a warden clerk called Pellam writes your names in his ledger, then writes them again.
"The captain has a table,"
he says.
"So we see it first,"
says Pellam.
"Whatever the mountain does, a warden writes it down. Most nights the log says nothing."
He looks proud.
"Nothing is the best thing a log can say."
A sign says ANYTHING THAT HUMS, LOG IT HERE. Pellam dips his pen and waits, like a cat at a mouse hole.
"I can log your packs,"
he says,
"or explain the records."
Pellam logs everything you show him, draws tiny pictures, and hands it all back. Then he stamps your hands LOGGED.
"Honest on paper,"
he says.
"The best kind."
The ink will last for days.
Pellam turns the big log around. Page after page of stones, four hundred years of them, each written down twice.
"Every one of them went somewhere,"
he says.
"Nobody ever wrote down where."
The newest page is full. So is the one before.
Pellam reads the tag on the Clerk's Stone. It is in his own handwriting.
"Logged at the bridge,"
he breathes.
"Carried up. Here."
He has to sit down. He writes HOME beside the stone and waves you on.
Pellam does not look up.
"The bridge is logged. I go where the ledgers are."
He writes your names a third time, in a tiny notebook for people he has met twice.
"Irregular. Entirely legal. This way."
At a long table of watch-logs and one humming stone waits Captain Orla Voss, who commands the Skywardens.
"Show us what the road taught you,"
she says.
"Then we'll show you what the logs say."
You lay the last two days on the table: moths facing away, wolves too cold to hunt, a crab guarding its warm ground, a whole hillside of stones humming one note.
"Everything up here is leaning away from the mountain,"
you say. Captain Voss pushes the oldest log across the table.
"So did we,"
she says.
"Four hundred years ago."
You lay out the moths, the wolves and the crab, and they go around and around and will not join up. Pellam clears his throat, very kindly, and opens the oldest log.
"It took us four hundred years,"
he says.
"You have had two days."
Your bigfoot points at one ledger in a different color, half hidden. Pellam looks caught stealing cookies.
"That one's not read. It's only kept."
Captain Voss holds out her hand. The room goes very quiet.
You describe the wounded glades, the MossHome path archive and the knot-cord. Pellam sets them beside the old watch-log.
"The forest keeps records too,"
says Voss.
"Custody,"
says Voss. Pellam adds it to both entries. The stone keeps humming on the table.
Voss circles three towns on her map.
"Acceptable losses,"
she says. Her voice is calm. The words are not.
"A town is not a number,"
you say. Voss looks at the map a long time.
"No. It's three numbers. Houses, people, bells."
Then, very quietly:
"I know."
She draws one circle a little smaller.
"One cup of tea before the record,"
says Pellam. From the window you see three kinds of light: Hessa's moving lantern, the glittering camps, and the bell towers of the dragonling towns. Which do you watch?
You look up, the way the whole citadel does. Over Mount Red Sky, the sky is a deep, wrong red. The mountain puffs out ash, slow, like somebody breathing in their sleep.
"Somebody writes that down every night,"
says Pellam softly.
"Tonight it's me."
Pellam opens a fresh page.
"What have you been doing, all this way?"
Tell it in your own words, or point to something you did.
Your first reason was finding out what happened.
"Today you did,"
says Pellam.
You came to prove you could.
"Here you are,"
says Pellam.
Pellam reads it all back and taps the page.
"Helping. Fixing. Putting things back where they belong. That adds up to one word, and the word is return."
Captain Voss raises one eyebrow, which for her is practically a parade.
Pellam reads it back, and the stone on the table hums along.
"Pockets,"
he says.
"A great many pockets. That adds up to a collection."
Nobody says he is wrong. A moth lands on your bag, thinks about it, and leaves.
Pellam reads it back slowly.
"Questions about what the power could do. Who holds it. What it's for."
He writes one word and underlines it twice: leash. Far below, Hessa's soup tent is still serving.
"Who should stand with you now?"
asks Voss.
"The wardens, the grandmothers' towns, or nobody else yet?"
If you made a promise on the road, you can keep it, or choose again after what you learned. She waits.
"Nobody else,"
says Captain Voss.
"Then you had better be right, and you had better be quick."
Pellam writes nothing at all, which he says later is the best entry a ledger can have.
"Grandmothers,"
sighs Captain Voss, like somebody who has argued with grandmothers before.
"Very well. They are at least thorough."
Pellam writes BELLS and underlines it. Far below, right on cue, one rings.
Captain Voss nods once, which is as much as she ever nods.
"Then you'll want the plan properly."
Pellam opens a fresh ledger with WARDENS AND PARTY on the spine. He has clearly had it ready for some time.
"And you? What is it all for?"
asks Voss. Return the stones, finish the collection, or learn to hold the power. At the mountain you will face this question again. Or say nothing for now, and leave on the return road.
"Hold it. The leash."
Voss and Pellam look at each other.
"Our plan, in fewer words,"
she says. Below the window, the soup-tent choir hums.
"Leash,"
Pellam says, and underlines it twice.
"Holding is harder than asking. You have to know you are choosing it."
Captain Voss closes the book.
"Helping. Fixing. Putting things back,"
Pellam reads.
"That is not the same as holding a leash,"
says Voss.
"Pockets. A great many pockets,"
Pellam reads.
"That is not the same as holding a leash,"
says Voss.
"Questions about the power, and who holds it,"
Pellam reads.
"You have been asking about the leash all the way up,"
says Voss.
"Finish the collection."
Voss considers it.
"Then I will write you down as weather."
Pellam writes WEATHER, then adds a question mark. The ink takes a long time to dry.
"Collection,"
Pellam says, and writes COLLECT in his neatest hand, with a small question mark. Captain Voss watches the ink dry.
"You will have to live up to that word,"
she says.
"Helping. Fixing. Putting things back,"
Pellam reads.
"That is a different word from the one you just said."
"Pockets. A great many pockets,"
he reads.
"Nobody can say you didn't warn us."
"Questions about the power, and who holds it,"
Pellam reads.
"That is a different word from the one you just said."
"Put it back. Every stone."
The table answers with one clear note. Voss unfolds her arms.
"Then we need the stones coming north tomorrow. Rest first."
"Put it back,"
Pellam says, and writes RETURN beside your names. He leaves a little space after it, in case the road teaches you something else. Captain Voss nods.
"Helping. Fixing. Putting things back,"
Pellam reads.
"The pages and the promise agree."
"Pockets. A great many pockets,"
Pellam reads.
"And now you say put it back. People do turn around,"
says Voss.
"Questions about the power, and who holds it,"
Pellam reads.
"And now you say put it back. People do turn around,"
says Voss.
Pellam writes RETURN, with a question mark.
"A starting road, then,"
says Voss.
"You can carry a question as well as a plan."
She leaves your earlier promises in the record.

You spend the night outside the gate. At midnight a little hatch opens. A warden clerk called Pellam passes out the old watch-logs by lantern and reads you the oldest line. The gemstones are pieces of a seal. The seal holds a titan asleep under Mount Red Sky. And the rush is taking it apart, one pocket at a time.
"What is it all for?"
he whispers. Take time to hear one another before answering.
"The return road, for now,"
Pellam whispers after your silence.
"The question stays open."
He passes a blanket through the hatch, then another.
"Hold it,"
you whisper.
"The leash."
The pen stops.
"That's my captain's word,"
Pellam whispers, puzzled. He passes out a blanket and a tiny book with CAGE on the spine, and asks for it back in the morning.
"Finish the collection,"
you whisper. There is a pause behind the hatch.
"Noted,"
Pellam whispers at last. After another pause, a blanket comes through anyway.
"Put it back,"
you whisper through the hatch. Pellam's pen scratches.
"Good,"
he whispers back, which is not a thing clerks say. A blanket follows the lantern.
A wagon wheel is stuck in a rut, blocking the road again.
"I'll pull, you push!"
says the centaur drover.
"On my heave!"
Everybody behind you offers excellent advice.
The wheel pops out like a cork. Forty drovers say it was their idea. The centaur drover gives you three coins.
"Toll refund. Do not ask which toll."
The drovers lean in beside you, and the wagon rocks free. The centaur drover gives you three coins.
"Toll refund."
You help Hessa's helpers carry the hot supper pots down the line. At the last tent, a tired prospector cups a bowl and stops shivering. Hessa wraps a supper for your pack.
"For the road,"
she says.
Bone crawlers clack up the cellar stairs, chasing the hum of the logged stones. They are beetles the size of bread loaves, fond of chewing table legs.
"Please get them downstairs before they find the old logs!"
says Pellam. His pen keeps moving.
The last crawler clacks downstairs. Pellam shuts the door and writes CRAWLERS: HOME. Then he gives you a tin whistle stamped with a tiny tower.
"Warden's issue. For loud moments. Log it if you use it."
He straightens his collar.
"Now, the tags."
A line of wardens marches in with brooms and sweeps the crawlers downstairs like autumn leaves. Nobody is hurt. Someone hands you hot tea. Pellam writes your names in the margin anyway.
"Now, the tags,"
he says.
Every humming thing in the citadel gets a picture tag.
"Watch them go by,"
says Pellam,
"then put them back in order. The captain likes order."
Moon, flame, leaf, flame. Pellam gives a tiny, rare smile.
"The captain will be thrilled,"
he says.
"She will not show it."
You swap two tags. Pellam sighs and fixes them with his pen.
"Order matters,"
he says kindly.
"It will do. The captain is waiting."
Pellam pours the tea. Captain Voss takes the smallest cup and drinks without a word. For a while the only question is Pellam's:
"More tea, anyone?"
Then he turns to a fresh page.
You plant your feet beside the grandmother. Nobody can dig up a doorstep with people on it. Dunmore goes pinker than ever.
"Sorry,"
he mumbles, and pulls up his flag. She gives him a cookie.
Grandmother Tull teaches the traveling call: one ring, two quick rings, one ring. Watch, then echo it.
"The ridge watch knows this one,"
she says.
"Ring it at the gate and they'll notice you."
Before you choose a road, everyone gets a turn. Say what you want to protect, what you still need to know, or what you are willing to try. Pellam puts down his pen.
"For once,"
he says,
"the ledger can wait."
